Docker: what is a *dangling* image?
column2:
An image layer with no tag, shown as <none>:<none>. It appears when you rebuild an image reusing the same tag: the tag moves to the NEW build, the old layers are left untagged = dangling.

`docker image prune` (no -a) removes exactly these.

column1: Docker: `docker image prune` vs `docker image prune -a`?
column2:
prune      = DANGLING images only (untagged <none>:<none>).
prune -a   = ALL images not referenced by any container (tagged ones included).

column1: Docker: does `docker image prune -a` delete an image a container uses?
column2: No. Any container reference protects the image — running OR stopped. Only images with zero container references are removed. (New CLI marks these 'In Use / U'.)

column1: Docker: what is an 'unused volume' (prune target)?
column2:
A volume referenced by NO container at prune time.

Gotcha: `docker compose down` (without -v) removes containers but KEEPS named volumes -> they become unused -> `docker volume prune -a` will then delete them.

column1: Docker: `docker volume prune` default vs `-a`?
column2:
default = only ANONYMOUS unused volumes.
-a      = also NAMED unused volumes (the dangerous one — eats DB volumes).

column1: Docker: does `docker system prune --volumes` remove NAMED volumes?
column2: No. It only removes ANONYMOUS unused volumes. Named unused volumes survive it entirely — you need `docker volume prune -a` for those.

column1: Docker: back up (and restore) a named volume to a tarball
column2:
# BACKUP: ephemeral alpine, volume read-only at /v, host cwd at /backup
docker run --rm -v <vol>:/v:ro -v "$PWD":/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/<vol>.tar.gz -C /v .

# RESTORE (reverse): volume writable, untar back in
docker run --rm -v <vol>:/v -v "$PWD":/backup \
  alpine sh -c 'tar xzf /backup/<vol>.tar.gz -C /v'

column1: Docker: why doesn't the `--rm` backup helper orphan the volume?
column2: Because the REAL owner container references the volume the whole time. The helper just adds a temporary 2nd link (LINKS 1->2); on exit --rm drops it back to 1. A volume is only a prune target when NO container references it.

column1: Docker: for a LIVE database, why not tar the volume?
column2:
A running DB has buffered/in-flight writes, so a file-level tar can be torn and inconsistent. Use a LOGICAL dump (transaction-consistent), or stop the container first.

# postgres (all DBs + roles). NO -t: a pty rewrites \n->\r\n and corrupts the dump.
docker exec <pg> pg_dumpall -U postgres > dump-$(date +%F).sql
# mysql — inline -p<pw> is world-readable in `ps` (argv); pass via env instead:
docker exec -e MYSQL_PWD=<pw> <mysql> mysqldump -u root <db> > db-$(date +%F).sql

column1: Docker: new `docker images` columns DISK USAGE vs CONTENT SIZE?
column2:
containerd image store output.
DISK USAGE   = unpacked size on disk (what occupies /var/lib/docker).
CONTENT SIZE = compressed blob size in the content store (~ download size).
IN USE (U)   = referenced by a container.
`docker image ls --tree` shows per-platform variants; 0B rows = platforms not pulled.

column1: Docker: why is `du /var/lib/docker` smaller than the sum of image sizes?
column2:
Docker reports LOGICAL sizes; `du` reports PHYSICAL blocks. On btrfs+zstd (CachyOS default) physical < logical. NOT shared-layer inflation if SHARED SIZE=0.

Confirm: findmnt -no FSTYPE,OPTIONS -T /var/lib/docker  (look for compress=zstd)
         sudo compsize /var/lib/docker                   (exact ratio, ~1.4x at zstd:1)

column1: Docker: how to untag / retag an image?
column2:
docker tag SRC NEW        # add a tag (an image can have many)
docker rmi NAME:TAG       # remove THAT tag; if other refs remain the image stays (just untagged), else it's deleted
There is no dedicated `docker untag` verb.

column1: Docker: fix the legacy-builder deprecation warning?
column2:
Install buildx so BuildKit becomes the default builder.
Arch/CachyOS:  sudo pacman -S docker-buildx
(reverse: sudo pacman -R docker-buildx). Then `docker build` uses BuildKit and the DEPRECATED notice goes away.

column1: Docker: in the volume-backup `tar`, what does `-C /v .` do (and where is the archive written)?
column2:
Two independent jobs:
- WHERE it's written: `-f /backup/x.tar.gz` (ABSOLUTE) — unaffected by -C or pwd.
- WHAT is packed: `-C /v` chdirs into /v, then `.` = its contents. `.` is the INPUT, not the output.

`-C /v .` records members as ./file (relative to /v), so `tar x -C /v` restores into the volume root. Plain `tar ... /v` records v/file -> restores to /v/v/file (wrong); GNU tar also warns "Removing leading '/'".

column1: Docker: what do `docker exec` flags `-i`, `-t`, `-e` do?
column2:
-i (--interactive) = keep the container's STDIN open — needed to PIPE data in (restore: cat x.sql | docker exec -i <c> psql). Without it: instant EOF -> silent no-op. A dump (output redirected out) does NOT need it.
-t (--tty) = allocate a pseudo-TTY; for an interactive shell (docker exec -it <c> bash).
-e (--env) = set an env var for that one exec (fresh env each call, so it repeats on the restore line). -e MYSQL_PWD=<pw> passes a secret via ENV, not argv — argv (/proc/<pid>/cmdline) is world-readable 0444, environ is owner-only 0400.

column1: Docker: why must you NOT use `docker exec -t` when redirecting output to a file?
column2: -t allocates a pseudo-TTY, and a pty maps \n -> \r\n on output. So `docker exec -t <c> pg_dumpall > dump.sql` writes CRLF-corrupted bytes and pg_restore can segfault on it. Drop -t for ANY redirect-to-file (dumps, binary output). Keep -t only for interactive shells (docker exec -it <c> bash).
